```python norun
df.mapInPandas(fn, schema)                     # iterate pandas batches per partition
pdf = df.limit(1000).toPandas()                 # small results only
sdf = spark.createDataFrame(pdf)                # pandas → Spark
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")   # faster
toPandas/createDataFrame
```

#### Choosing

1. Built-in functions (always first)

2. Spark SQL expressions / higher-order functions

3. pandas UDF / applyInPandas

4. Python UDF

title: Partitioning
md:
> **In simple words:** partitioning is about how data is split — when it's read (input partitions), after a shuffle (shuffle partitions), and how it's stored in folders (storage partitions). Get the sizes right (~100–200 MB per partition) and Spark uses every core without running out of memory.

**Memory hook:** Repartition = Reshuffle (both start with R — full shuffle, can go up or down). Coalesce = Combine (both start with C — merge neighbours, only down).

#### Three kinds of "partitioning"

| Kind | What | Controlled by |
|---|---|---|
| Input partitions | How files are split into tasks when reading | `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` (128 MB), file count and sizes |
| Shuffle partitions | Number of tasks after a shuffle | `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` (200), AQE coalescing |
| Storage partitions | Folder layout on disk (`partitionBy`) | Your write code |

#### Checking partitions

```python norun
df.rdd.getNumPartitions()
df.groupBy(F.spark_partition_id()).count().show()     # rows per partition — spot skew
```

#### repartition vs coalesce

|  | `repartition(n)` / `repartition("col")` | `coalesce(n)` |
|---|---|---|
| Can increase partitions | Yes | No |
| Shuffle | Full shuffle | No shuffle (merges neighbours) |
| Result | Even sizes; by-column puts each key in one partition | Can be uneven |
| Use for | Fix skew/parallelism, prepare for `partitionBy` writes, joins | Reduce file count before writing |

> `coalesce(1)` before writing forces the entire upstream stage onto one task in many plans. Use it only for tiny outputs.

#### Sizing shuffle partitions

Aim for ~100–200 MB per shuffle partition. For 500 GB of shuffle data that's roughly 2,500– 5,000 partitions; for 2 GB, the default 200 is too many. With AQE enabled, set a reasonably high initial number and let AQE coalesce small partitions.

#### Partition pruning and predicate pushdown

- **Partition pruning:** filters on storage-partition columns skip whole folders.
- **Predicate pushdown:** filters on other columns are pushed to the file reader; Parquet/ORC skip row groups using min/max statistics.
- **Column pruning:** only selected columns are read from columnar files.

```python norun
df = spark.read.parquet("/silver/orders")
df.filter("order_date = '2026-01-15' AND amount > 1000").select("order_id", "amount").explain()
# PartitionFilters: [order_date = 2026-01-15]   PushedFilters: [GreaterThan(amount,1000)]
```

Functions on the partition column (`year(order_date) = 2026`) can block pruning — filter the raw column with a range.

#### Choosing a storage partition column

- Used in most filters (usually a date).
- Low to medium cardinality — thousands of partitions at most, not millions.
- Each partition should hold enough data for decent file sizes. Partitioning a 10 GB table by day for 10 years gives ~3 MB per day — too small; partition by month or not at all, and use clustering instead.

title: Caching and persistence
md:
#### When to cache

> **In simple words:** Spark forgets results after each action and recomputes from the start next time. Caching says "keep this result in memory because I'll use it again". Useful when reused; wasteful when used once.

**Memory hook:** the **fridge** — put food in only if you'll eat it again soon, and clear it out after (`unpersist`). Cache is the Common default; Persist lets you Pick the level.

Cache a DataFrame when it is **reused by multiple actions** and is expensive to recompute — for example a cleaned dataset that feeds three different aggregations.

```text
clean = raw.filter(...).dropDuplicates(["id"]).cache()
clean.count()                         # materializes the cache
clean.groupBy("city").count().write...
clean.groupBy("status").count().write...
clean.unpersist()
```

#### Storage levels

| Level | Where | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `MEMORY_ONLY` | Memory, deserialized | Fastest; partitions that don't fit are recomputed |
| `MEMORY_AND_DISK` | Memory, spill to disk | `df.cache()` default for DataFrames |
| `MEMORY_ONLY_SER` / `MEMORY_AND_DISK_SER` | Serialized | Less memory, more CPU (RDD API) |
| `DISK_ONLY` | Disk | When memory is tight |
| `OFF_HEAP` | Off-heap memory | Needs config |

```python norun
from pyspark import StorageLevel
df.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)
```

#### Don't cache by default

- Caching costs memory that execution needs; over-caching causes spills and OOMs.
- A DataFrame used once gains nothing from caching.
- Caching is lazy — it fills on the first action.
- Always `unpersist()` when done in long jobs.
- On Databricks, the disk cache speeds up repeated reads of the same files automatically.

#### Checkpointing

```python norun
spark.sparkContext.setCheckpointDir("/tmp/checkpoints")
df = df.checkpoint()          # writes data, truncates lineage
df = df.localCheckpoint()     # executor-local, faster, less safe
```

Use checkpointing for very long lineages (iterative loops) where the plan itself becomes slow to optimize, or recomputation after failure would be huge.

title: Catalyst, Tungsten and Adaptive Query Execution
md:
> **In simple words: Catalyst** rewrites your query into a faster equivalent before it runs (like a GPS finding a better route). **Tungsten** makes the engine itself efficient (compact memory, generated code). **AQE** changes the route while driving, using real traffic data from the parts of the job already finished.

**Memory hook — the three helpers: Catalyst** = the planner (before the trip), **Tungsten** = the engine (how fast the car runs), **AQE** = live traffic updates (during the trip).

#### Catalyst optimizer

Every DataFrame or SQL query goes through:

1. **Unresolved logical plan** — parsed, names not checked.

2. **Analyzed logical plan** — columns and tables resolved against the catalog.

3. **Optimized logical plan** — rule-based rewrites: predicate pushdown, column pruning, constant folding, combining filters, simplifying expressions.

4. **Physical plans** — candidate execution strategies (e.g. broadcast vs sort-merge join), chosen with cost estimates.

5. **Code generation** — whole-stage codegen compiles parts of the plan into Java bytecode.

```python norun
df.explain()                     # physical plan
df.explain(mode="extended")      # all plans
df.explain(mode="formatted")     # readable sections
df.explain(mode="cost")          # with statistics
```

What to look for in a plan:

- `Exchange` = shuffle. Count them.
- `BroadcastHashJoin` vs `SortMergeJoin`.
- `PushedFilters`, `PartitionFilters` in the scan.
- `*(1)` stars = whole-stage codegen.
- `BatchEvalPython` / `ArrowEvalPython` = Python UDFs.

#### Tungsten

Tungsten is Spark's execution layer: compact binary row format, off-heap memory management, cache-aware algorithms and generated code. It's why DataFrames are much faster than RDDs of Python objects.

#### Adaptive Query Execution (AQE)

AQE re-optimizes the plan **during** execution using real statistics collected at shuffle boundaries. Enabled by default since Spark 3.2.

| Feature | What it does | Config |
|---|---|---|
| Coalesce shuffle partitions | Merges small post-shuffle partitions into fewer, right- sized ones | `spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled` |
| Switch join strategy | Converts sort-merge to broadcast when a side turns out small | automatic |
| Skew join | Splits oversized partitions in sort-merge joins | `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled` |
| Local shuffle reader | Avoids network reads after converting to broadcast | automatic |

```python norun
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes", "128m")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor", "5")
```

#### Dynamic Partition Pruning (DPP)

When a partitioned fact table is joined to a filtered dimension, Spark uses the dimension's filter result at runtime to prune fact partitions:

```sql norun
SELECT ... FROM sales s JOIN dim_date d ON s.sale_date = d.date
WHERE d.fiscal_quarter = 'FY26-Q1'      -- only matching sale_date partitions are read
```

#### Statistics

The optimizer's choices depend on size and cardinality estimates. Keep table statistics fresh (`ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE STATISTICS`), especially for broadcast decisions without AQE.

title: Memory and cluster sizing
md:
> **In simple words:** each executor has a fixed memory budget. Part of it is for running tasks (shuffles, joins, sorts), part for cached data, and some extra outside the JVM for Python and overheads. Most "out of memory" errors mean one task got too much data — usually because of too few partitions or skew — not that the cluster is too small.

**Memory hook:** "OOM on the driver = too much came to the boss (collect, big broadcast). OOM on an executor = one basket was too heavy (skew, too few partitions)."

#### Executor memory layout

```text
spark.executor.memory  (JVM heap)
├── Reserved memory              ~300 MB
├── User memory                  (1 - spark.memory.fraction)  ~40%: your objects,
UDF data structures
└── Unified memory               spark.memory.fraction = 0.6
    ├── Execution memory         shuffles, joins, sorts, aggregations
    └── Storage memory           cache, broadcast variables
        (spark.memory.storageFraction = 0.5 is protected from eviction; the
boundary moves)
+ spark.executor.memoryOverhead  off-heap: JVM overhead, Python workers, network
buffers (default max(384MB, 10%))
```

Execution can borrow from storage (evicting cached blocks) and vice versa within the unified region.

#### Sizing executors

Common starting point on YARN/Kubernetes:

- **4–5 cores per executor** (more cores per JVM increases GC and I/O contention).
- Memory per executor = (node memory − OS overhead) / executors per node, minus memoryOverhead.
- Leave a core and some memory per node for the OS and node manager.
- PySpark with UDFs/pandas UDFs needs more `memoryOverhead`, because Python workers live outside the JVM heap.

On Databricks you mostly pick node types and worker counts; Spark configs are derived for you.

#### Dynamic allocation

```text
spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=true
spark.dynamicAllocation.minExecutors=2
spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors=50
```

Executors are added when tasks are pending and removed when idle. Needs shuffle tracking or an external shuffle service.

#### Out of memory: driver vs executor

| Where | Typical causes | Fixes |
|---|---|---|
| Driver | `collect()`/`toPandas()` on big data, broadcasting large tables, huge numbers of small files/partitions to plan, very large plans | Write instead of collect, don't broadcast big tables, compact files, increase driver memory last |
| Executor Skewed partitions, too few shuffle partitions | (huge partitions), big `collect_list`/explode, large Python UDF batches, over-caching | More/even partitions, fix skew, AQE, reduce cached data, raise memoryOverhead for Python |

#### Spill

When execution memory runs out, Spark spills sorted/hashed data to disk. Some spill is normal; heavy spill (visible in the Spark UI as "Spill (Memory)" and "Spill (Disk)") means partitions are too big — increase partition count or memory.

#### Garbage collection

Long GC times (shown per task in the Spark UI) point to memory pressure: too many cores sharing a heap, very large objects, or too much cached data. Use fewer cores per executor, smaller partitions, or serialized caching.

title: Performance playbook
md:
#### Read less

- Columnar formats (Parquet/Delta), with compression.
- Select only needed columns early.
- Filter early, on partition columns where possible.
- Partition and cluster tables for the common filters.

#### Shuffle less

- Broadcast small dimension tables.
- Aggregate before joining when it reduces rows.
- Avoid unnecessary `distinct`, `orderBy`, `repartition`.
- Reuse the same partitioning for consecutive operations on the same key.
- Bucket or cluster large tables joined repeatedly on the same key.

#### Balance work

- Right-size shuffle partitions (AQE helps).
- Detect skew (Spark UI: max task time far above median) and fix it: AQE skew join, broadcast, isolate hot keys, salting.
- Avoid windows without `partitionBy`.

#### Avoid Python overhead

- Built-in functions over UDFs; pandas UDFs over Python UDFs.
- No `collect()` in loops; no per-row Python logic on the driver.

#### Keep plans healthy

- No `withColumn` in long loops — use one `select`.
- Checkpoint very long iterative lineages.
- Avoid repeated `count()` calls used only for logging on huge DataFrames; each is a full job.

#### Fix the small-file problem

Thousands of tiny files slow down listing, planning and reading.

- Repartition by the partition column before writing.
- Compact with Delta `OPTIMIZE`, auto-compaction or optimized writes.
- Batch streaming writes with sensible triggers.

#### Common anti-patterns

| Anti-pattern | Better |
|---|---|
| `df.collect()` then loop in Python | Express the logic with DataFrame operations |
| `inferSchema` on large CSV in production | Explicit schema |
| `coalesce(1)` for big outputs | Repartition to sensible file sizes |
| Python UDF for string cleaning | `regexp_replace`, `trim`, `lower` |
| `union` of many small DataFrames in a loop | Read all files in one `spark.read` |
| Joining on mismatched types | Cast once, join on matching types |
| Caching everything | Cache only reused, expensive DataFrames |

title: Reading the Spark UI
md:
#### Tabs

| Tab | Shows |
|---|---|
| Jobs | One row per action; duration, stages, status |
| Stages | Tasks per stage, input/output, shuffle read/write, spill; task-time distribution |
| Storage | Cached DataFrames, size in memory/disk |
| Environment | All Spark configs actually in effect |
| Executors | Memory, cores, task counts, GC time, shuffle per executor; failed executors |
| SQL / DataFrame | Query plans with per-operator metrics (rows, time, size) |
| Structured Streaming | Input rate, processing rate, batch duration, state size |

#### Diagnosing from the UI

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| One or a few tasks take much longer than the median | Skew |
| Large "Spill (Disk)" | Partitions too big for memory |
| Thousands of tasks of a few KB each | Too many small partitions/files |
| Few tasks while many cores sit idle | Too few partitions |
| High GC time | Memory pressure |
| Huge shuffle write | A wide transformation you might avoid (broadcast, pre-aggregate) |
| Long gap before tasks start | File listing, driver-side planning, many small files |
| Executors lost / tasks retried | OOM or node failure — check executor logs |

> Compare a fast run and a slow run of the same job side by side: input size, number of tasks, shuffle sizes and max task time usually point straight at the cause.

title: Structured Streaming
md:
#### The model

> **In simple words:** Structured Streaming runs your normal DataFrame code again and again on small batches of new data (every few seconds or minutes), remembering where it stopped in a **checkpoint**. You write it almost like batch code; Spark handles the "only process new data" part.

**Memory hook — exactly-once is "R·C·I", Really Careful Ingestion: R**eplayable source + **C**heckpoint + **I**dempotent sink. Miss one and you get duplicates or gaps.

A stream is treated as an **unbounded table**. Each trigger, new rows are appended to the input table, your query runs incrementally on them, and results are written to the sink. You use the same DataFrame API as batch.

#### Sources and sinks

| Sources | Sinks |
|---|---|
| Kafka, Event Hubs (Kafka API), Kinesis | Delta, Parquet/files |
| Files arriving in a folder (Auto Loader on Databricks) | Kafka |
| Delta tables (as a stream) | `foreachBatch` (any batch writer: JDBC, MERGE) |
| Rate source (testing) | Console, memory (testing) |

#### A complete Kafka → Delta stream

```python norun
schema = "event_id STRING, user_id STRING, event_ts TIMESTAMP, action STRING"
raw = (spark.readStream.format("kafka")
       .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker:9092")
       .option("subscribe", "clicks")
       .option("startingOffsets", "latest")
       .option("maxOffsetsPerTrigger", 500_000)
       .load())
events = (raw.select(F.from_json(F.col("value").cast("string"), schema).alias("e"))
             .select("e.*"))
q = (events.writeStream
     .format("delta")
     .outputMode("append")
     .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/clicks_bronze")
     .trigger(processingTime="1 minute")
     .toTable("bronze.clicks"))
q.awaitTermination()
```

#### Triggers

| Trigger | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| default (none) | Next micro-batch starts as soon as the previous finishes |
| `processingTime="1 minute"` | Micro-batch every interval |
| `availableNow=True` | Process everything available now in batches, then stop — great for scheduled "incremental batch" jobs |
| `once=True` | Older single-batch version of availableNow |
| `continuous="1 second"` | Experimental low-latency mode, limited operations |

#### Output modes

| Mode | Emits | Use with |
|---|---|---|
| `append` | Only new final rows | Stateless queries; windowed aggregations with a watermark |
| `update` | Rows changed in this batch | Aggregations where the sink supports upserts |
| `complete` The whole result table each | batch | Small aggregations only |

#### Checkpoints

The checkpoint location stores source offsets, state and commit logs. It is what lets a stream restart exactly where it stopped.

- One unique checkpoint per query; never share between queries.
- Don't delete it casually — the stream will reprocess from `startingOffsets`.
- Some query changes (different aggregations, changed stateful operators) are incompatible with an existing checkpoint.

#### Event time, watermarks and windows

```text
counts = (events
          .withWatermark("event_ts", "15 minutes")
          .groupBy(F.window("event_ts", "10 minutes"), "action")
          .count())
```

- **Event time:** when the event happened (inside the data). **Processing time:** when Spark sees it.
- **Watermark:** "I don't expect events older than max(event_ts) − 15 minutes". Spark keeps state for windows only until the watermark passes them, then finalizes and drops the state. Events later than the watermark are dropped.
- Window types: tumbling `window(ts, "10 minutes")`, sliding `window(ts, "10 minutes", "5` `minutes")`, session `session_window(ts, "30 minutes")`.

#### Stateful operations

Aggregations, stream-stream joins, deduplication and `applyInPandasWithState` keep state across batches. Without a watermark, state grows forever. Use the RocksDB state store for large state:

```python norun
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass",
               "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider")
```

#### Deduplication

```text
deduped = (events.withWatermark("event_ts", "30 minutes")
                 .dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"]))      # Spark 3.5+
# older: .dropDuplicates(["event_id", "event_ts"]) with a watermark
```

#### Stream-static and stream-stream joins

```text
enriched = events.join(broadcast(dim_users), "user_id", "left")      # stream-static: dim re-read
per batch (Delta)
joined = (impressions.withWatermark("imp_ts", "1 hour")
          .join(clicks.withWatermark("click_ts", "2 hours"),
                F.expr("""click_ad_id = imp_ad_id AND
                          click_ts BETWEEN imp_ts AND imp_ts + interval 1 hour""")))
```

Stream-stream joins need watermarks on both sides and a time-range condition so state can be cleaned up.

#### foreachBatch: run batch logic per micro-batch

```python norun
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
def upsert(batch_df, batch_id):
    latest = (batch_df.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(
                  W.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.desc("updated_at"))))
              .filter("rn = 1").drop("rn"))
    (DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.orders").alias("t")
       .merge(latest.alias("s"), "t.order_id = s.order_id")
       .whenMatchedUpdateAll()
       .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
       .execute())
(orders_stream.writeStream
   .foreachBatch(upsert)
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/orders_silver")
   .trigger(availableNow=True)
   .start())
```

`foreachBatch` lets you use MERGE, JDBC writes, or write one batch to several sinks.

#### Exactly-once

End-to-end exactly-once needs all three:

1. A **replayable source** (Kafka offsets, files, Delta).

2. **Checkpointed** progress.

3. An **idempotent or transactional sink** (Delta, or MERGE by key in `foreachBatch`; use `batch_id` to skip already-committed batches when writing elsewhere).

Kafka sinks are at-least-once — downstream consumers should deduplicate.

#### Monitoring and operations

```python norun
q.status; q.lastProgress; q.recentProgress
spark.streams.active
q.stop()
```

Watch input rate vs processing rate (falling behind?), batch duration vs trigger interval, and state size. Alert when a query stops or lags.

title: Testing and data quality
md:
#### Local SparkSession for tests

```python norun
# tests/conftest.py
import pytest
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def spark():
    s = (SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").appName("tests")
         .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "2").getOrCreate())
    yield s
    s.stop()
```

#### Testing a transformation

```python norun
from pyspark.testing import assertDataFrameEqual      # Spark 3.5+
def test_latest_per_key(spark):
    df = spark.createDataFrame(
        [(1, "A", "2026-01-01"), (1, "B", "2026-01-02"), (2, "C", "2026-01-01")],
        "id INT, city STRING, updated_at STRING")
    expected = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "B"), (2, "C")], "id INT, city STRING")
    assertDataFrameEqual(latest_per_key(df).select("id", "city"), expected)
```

Before 3.5, compare `sorted(df.collect())` lists, or use the `chispa` library.

#### In-pipeline checks

```python norun
def check(df, name):
    total = df.count()
    dupes = df.groupBy("order_id").count().filter("count > 1").count()
    nulls = df.filter(F.col("order_id").isNull()).count()
    if dupes or nulls:
        raise ValueError(f"{name}: {dupes} duplicate keys, {nulls} null keys out of {total}")
```

Compute several metrics in one aggregation to avoid many separate jobs:

```python norun
m = df.agg(F.count("*").alias("rows"),
           F.countDistinct("order_id").alias("keys"),
           F.sum(F.col("order_id").isNull().cast("int")).alias("null_keys")).first()
```

Libraries: Great Expectations, Deequ / PyDeequ, Soda, and Delta Live Tables expectations on Databricks.

title: Common pipeline patterns
md:
#### Bronze → silver cleaning

```python norun
silver = (spark.read.table("bronze.orders")
  .withColumn("order_id", F.col("order_id").cast("bigint"))
  .withColumn("amount", F.col("amount").cast("decimal(18,2)"))
  .withColumn("order_ts", F.to_timestamp("order_ts"))
  .withColumn("order_date", F.to_date("order_ts"))
  .withColumn("email", F.lower(F.trim("email")))
  .filter(F.col("order_id").isNotNull())
  .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(
      W.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.desc("updated_at"), F.desc("_ingest_ts"))))
  .filter("rn = 1").drop("rn"))
```

#### Upsert into Delta (SCD Type 1)

```python norun
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
t = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.customers")
(t.alias("t").merge(updates.alias("s"), "t.customer_id = s.customer_id")
   .whenMatchedUpdateAll(condition="t.row_hash <> s.row_hash")
   .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
   .execute())
```

#### SCD Type 2 with Delta MERGE (single statement)

```python norun
cur = spark.table("gold.dim_customer").filter("is_current")
changed = (updates.alias("s").join(cur.alias("c"), "customer_id")
           .filter("s.row_hash <> c.row_hash").select("s.*"))
staged = (changed.withColumn("merge_key", F.lit(None).cast("bigint"))          # rows to insert
as new versions
          .unionByName(updates.withColumn("merge_key", F.col("customer_id"))))  # rows to
match/close or insert
(DeltaTable.forName(spark, "gold.dim_customer").alias("t")
  .merge(staged.alias("s"), "t.customer_id = s.merge_key AND t.is_current = true")
  .whenMatchedUpdate(condition="t.row_hash <> s.row_hash",
                     set={"is_current": "false", "valid_to": "s.load_ts"})
  .whenNotMatchedInsert(values={
      "customer_id": "s.customer_id", "city": "s.city", "row_hash": "s.row_hash",
      "valid_from": "s.load_ts", "valid_to": "null", "is_current": "true"})
  .execute())
```

Changed customers appear twice in `staged`: once with their key (to close the old row) and once with a NULL key (never matches, so it inserts the new version). New customers match nothing and insert. Unchanged customers match but fail the update condition.

#### Incremental processing

```python norun
last = spark.table("silver.orders").agg(F.max("updated_at")).first()[0]
inc = spark.table("bronze.orders")
if last is not None:
    inc = inc.filter(F.col("updated_at") > F.lit(last) - F.expr("INTERVAL 1 HOUR"))   # overlap for
late rows
# dedup + MERGE inc
```

Alternatives on Delta: Change Data Feed (`readChangeFeed`), or Structured Streaming with `availableNow` over the bronze table — Spark tracks what was processed in the checkpoint.

#### Applying CDC events in order

```python norun
w = W.partitionBy("id").orderBy(F.desc("op_ts"))
latest = cdc.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("rn = 1")
(target.alias("t").merge(latest.alias("s"), "t.id = s.id")
  .whenMatchedDelete(condition="s.op = 'D'")
  .whenMatchedUpdateAll(condition="s.op <> 'D'")
  .whenNotMatchedInsertAll(condition="s.op <> 'D'")
  .execute())
```

#### Explode and flatten nested JSON

```text
orders = (raw.select(F.from_json("value", schema).alias("o")).select("o.*")
             .select("order_id", "customer.*", F.explode_outer("items").alias("item"))
             .select("order_id", "name", "city", "item.sku", "item.qty", "item.price"))
```

#### Sessionization

```text
w = W.partitionBy("user_id").orderBy("ts")
sessions = (clicks
  .withColumn("gap", F.col("ts").cast("long") - F.lag(F.col("ts").cast("long")).over(w))
  .withColumn("new", F.when(F.col("gap").isNull() | (F.col("gap") > 1800), 1).otherwise(0))
  .withColumn("session_id", F.concat_ws("-", "user_id", F.sum("new").over(w))))
```

#### Calendar fill

```text
bounds = sales.groupBy("store_id").agg(F.min("sale_date").alias("s"), F.max("sale_date").alias("e"))
cal = bounds.select("store_id", F.explode(F.sequence("s", "e")).alias("sale_date"))
full = cal.join(sales, ["store_id", "sale_date"], "left").fillna(0, ["amount"])
```

title: Submitting and deploying Spark jobs
md:
#### spark-submit

```python norun
spark-submit \
  --master yarn \
  --deploy-mode cluster \
  --name orders_daily \
  --num-executors 10 \
  --executor-cores 4 \
  --executor-memory 16g \
  --driver-memory 8g \
  --conf spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=400 \
  --conf spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=false \
  --py-files deps.zip \
  --packages io.delta:delta-spark_2.12:3.2.0 \
  main.py --run-date 2026-01-15
```

#### Packaging Python code

- Small projects: `--py-files` with a zip of your package.
- Better: build a wheel and install it on the cluster (Databricks libraries, cluster init scripts, or a custom image).
- Third-party Python libraries must be installed on **every** executor, not only the driver.

#### Job structure for production

```python norun
def main(run_date: str):
    spark = SparkSession.builder.appName(f"orders_{run_date}").getOrCreate()
    raw = extract(spark, run_date)
    clean = transform(raw)
    validate(clean)
    load(clean, run_date)          # idempotent: replaceWhere / MERGE
if __name__ == "__main__":
    import sys
    main(sys.argv[sys.argv.index("--run-date") + 1])
```

- Parameterize by run date; never use `current_date()` for which data to process.
- Keep transforms as functions of DataFrames → DataFrames, so they're testable with small local data.
- Make the load idempotent, so the orchestrator can retry safely.
- Log row counts and key metrics at each step.

> The core habit for Spark: think about **how data moves**. Before running a job on big data, look at the plan — how many shuffles, which join strategies, how many partitions — and ask if each shuffle is really needed.

title: Common beginner mistakes
md:
Almost everyone makes these when starting with Spark. Knowing them saves days of debugging.

| Mistake | What happens | Do this instead |
|---|---|---|
| Treating Spark like pandas: `collect()` / `toPandas()` on big data | All data goes to the driver → driver out of memory | Keep data distributed; write results, or `limit()` before collecting |
| Looping over rows in Python (`for row in df.collect()`) | Slow, single-machine, defeats Spark | Express logic with DataFrame functions, joins and windows |
| Using Python UDFs for simple logic | 5–10× slower, no optimization | `when/otherwise`, `regexp_replace`, built-in functions |
| `inferSchema=True` in production | Extra full read; wrong types (IDs lose leading zeros) | Explicit schema |
| `mode("overwrite")` on a partitioned table for one day | Whole table replaced with one day | Dynamic partition overwrite or Delta `replaceWhere` |
| `union` instead of `unionByName` | Columns silently mixed up when order differs | `unionByName(..., allowMissingColumns=True)` |
| `and` / `or` / `not` in filters | Python error or wrong logic | `&`, `\|`, `~` with parentheses around each condition |
| `dropDuplicates(["id"])` to "keep the latest" | Keeps an arbitrary row | `row_number()` over a window ordered by timestamp |
| Calling `count()` everywhere for logging | Each count is a full job on the whole data | Count once, or compute several metrics in one `agg` |
| `coalesce(1)` before writing big output | One task does all the work, very slow | Repartition to sensible file sizes |
| Caching everything | Memory pressure, spills, OOM | Cache only reused, expensive DataFrames, then `unpersist()` |
| Ignoring the Spark UI | Guessing at performance problems | Check skew, spill, shuffle size and task times first |
| `withColumn` in a loop over hundreds of columns | Huge plans, slow analysis | One `select` with a list of expressions |
| Joining on columns with different types | Implicit casts, wrong or missing matches | Cast once so both sides match |
| Not handling NULL join keys | NULLs never match; many NULLs create a skewed partition | Filter or handle NULL keys separately |
| `datetime.now()` / `current_date()` to decide which data to process | Reruns and backfills process the wrong day | Pass `run_date` as a parameter |
| Deleting or sharing a streaming checkpoint | Reprocessing, duplicates, or broken queries | One checkpoint per query, never touched casually |

> Most of these come from the same root cause: forgetting that Spark is distributed. Ask two questions about every line you write: where does this run (driver or executors)? and does this move data between machines?

title: Cluster sizing scenarios: 10 GB to 2 TB per day
md:
Sizing a Spark cluster is an estimate you make from a few numbers, then confirm with a test run and the Spark UI. Interviewers mainly want to see that you have a **method** and know which numbers matter.

#### Step 1: write down the assumptions

| Assumption | Value used in these scenarios |
|---|---|
| Daily input | 10 GB, 100 GB, 500 GB, 1 TB, 2 TB of **compressed Parquet/Delta** |
| Job shape | Read → clean/filter → join with dimensions (broadcast where small) → aggregate → write Delta. About **3 heavy stages** |
| Input partition size | 128 MB (`spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes`) |
| Time per task | ~1 minute to process a 128 MB partition through a heavy stage (typical ETL; simpler jobs or Photon are faster) |
| Target runtime | ~10–40 minutes depending on size (the batch window / SLA) |
| Shuffle size | About the same as the input (join + aggregation), target ~200 MB per shuffle partition |
| Worker node | **16 vCPU, 128 GB RAM** (memory-optimized, e.g. Azure E16s_v5 / AWS r5.4xlarge) |

> If the input is raw CSV/JSON instead of Parquet, the same data is several times larger on disk and parsing costs more CPU. Convert to Parquet/Delta in the bronze step, then size the heavy jobs on the Parquet size.

#### Step 2: executor layout per node

| Item | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Usable cores per node | 16 − 1 (OS, NodeManager/daemons) | **15** |
| Cores per executor | Rule of thumb 4–5 (good HDFS/ABFS throughput, less GC pressure) | **5** |
| Executors per node | 15 / 5 | **3** |
| Usable memory per node | 128 GB − ~8 GB (OS, daemons) | **~120 GB** |
| Memory per executor container | 120 / 3 | **40 GB** |
| memoryOverhead | max(384 MB, 10% of heap) | **~4 GB** |
| `spark.executor.memory` (heap) | 40 − 4 | **36 GB** |
| Unified (execution + storage) memory | (36 GB − 300 MB) × 0.6 | **~21 GB per executor** **≈ 4.3 GB per running** **task** |

4.3 GB per task is plenty for 128–200 MB partitions, even after they expand 3–4× in memory. That headroom is what avoids spills and OOMs.

#### Step 3: the formulas

```text
input_partitions   = input_size / 128 MB
core_minutes       = input_partitions × heavy_stages × minutes_per_task
cores_needed       = core_minutes / target_runtime_minutes
executors          = cores_needed / 5
worker_nodes       = executors / 3            (15 usable cores per node)
waves              = input_partitions / total_cores     (aim for a handful, not
100s)
shuffle_partitions = shuffle_size / ~200 MB   (round to a multiple of total cores)
```

#### Step 4: the five scenarios

| Daily input | Input tasks (÷128 MB) | Target runtime | Cores needed | Worker Executors nodes (5 cores, (16c/128 36 GB) GB) | Waves Total per cores stage | Shuffle Driver partitions |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **10 GB** 80 |  | ~10 min | 24 | **2** 6 | 30 ~3 | 64–100 4 (or AQE cores, from 200) 8 GB |
| **100** **GB** | 800 | ~30 min | 80 | **6** 18 | 90 ~9 | 500–720 8 cores, 16 GB |
| **500** **GB** | 4,000 | ~40 min | 300 | **20** 60 | 300 ~13 | 2,500– 8 3,000 cores, 16–32 GB |
| **1 TB** | 8,000 | ~40 min | 600 | **40** 120 | 600 ~13 | 5,000– 16 6,000 cores, 32 GB |
| **2 TB** | 16,000 | ~40 min | 1,200 | **80** 240 | 1,200 ~13 | 10,000– 16 12,000 cores, 32–64 GB |

How to read the trade-off: cores × time is roughly constant. If the SLA for 1 TB is 80 minutes instead of 40, ~20 nodes are enough; if it must finish in 20 minutes, you need ~80 nodes (and the job must have enough partitions to use them).

#### Worked example: 1 TB per day, 40-minute window

1. **Input partitions:** 1,000 GB ÷ 128 MB ≈ 8,000 tasks per heavy stage.

2. **Work:** 8,000 tasks × 3 heavy stages × ~1 min = 24,000 core-minutes.

3. **Cores:** 24,000 ÷ 40 min = **600 cores**.

4. **Executors:** 600 ÷ 5 = **120 executors** of 5 cores / 36 GB heap / 4 GB overhead.

5. **Nodes:** 120 ÷ 3 = **40 worker nodes** of 16 vCPU / 128 GB.

6. **Waves:** 8,000 ÷ 600 ≈ 13 waves per stage, ~13 minutes per stage, ~40 minutes total.

7. **Shuffle partitions:** ~1 TB shuffle ÷ 200 MB ≈ 5,000 → round to a multiple of 600 cores → **6,000** (with AQE coalescing on).

8. **Shuffle disk:** ~1 TB of shuffle files spread over 40 nodes ≈ 25 GB per node — make sure local disks (ideally SSD) have room, plus spill headroom.

9. **Driver:** 16 cores / 32 GB — planning 8,000+ tasks and broadcasting dimensions needs more than the default.

```python norun
spark-submit \
  --master yarn --deploy-mode cluster \
  --num-executors 120 \
  --executor-cores 5 \
  --executor-memory 36g \
  --conf spark.executor.memoryOverhead=4g \
  --driver-cores 16 --driver-memory 32g \
  --conf spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=6000 \
  --conf spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true \
  --conf spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled=true \
  --conf spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true \
  --conf spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold=100m \
  orders_daily.py --run-date 2026-01-15
```

On Databricks you'd pick ~40 workers of a 16-core/128 GB node type (or autoscale 20–50), and let Databricks set executor layout; keep AQE on and set shuffle partitions explicitly or to `auto`.

#### The classic interview calculation

"You have 10 nodes, each with 16 cores and 64 GB RAM. How many executors, and with what settings?"

| Step | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Usable per node | 16 − 1 core, 64 − 1 GB | 15 cores, 63 GB |
| Executors per node | 15 cores ÷ 5 | 3 |
| Total executors | 10 × 3 = 30, minus 1 for the YARN ApplicationMaster/driver | **29** |
| Memory per executor | 63 GB ÷ 3 | 21 GB |
| Overhead | ~7–10% of 21 GB | ~2 GB |
| `--executor- memory` | 21 − 2 | **~19 GB** |
| Final |  | `--num-executors 29 --executor- cores 5 --executor-memory 19g` |

Why not 1 executor with 15 cores per node? Large heaps mean long GC pauses and poor HDFS/ABFS throughput per JVM. Why not 15 executors with 1 core? No parallelism inside a JVM, broadcast variables copied 15 times per node, and per-JVM overhead wasted. 4–5 cores per executor is the middle ground.

#### What changes the numbers

| Factor | Effect on sizing |
|---|---|
| Skew | A single hot key makes one task run for an hour — more nodes won't help. Fix skew first (AQE, salting, broadcast) |
| Heavy Python UDFs | More CPU per task, more memoryOverhead for Python workers |
| Wide joins without broadcast | Larger shuffles → more shuffle partitions, more disk |
| Caching large DataFrames | Needs more storage memory — or a smaller cache |
| Raw JSON/CSV | More CPU and bytes than Parquet; parse once into bronze |
| Photon / vectorized engines | Fewer cores for the same SLA |
| Incremental processing | Processing only new/changed data shrinks every number above |
| Spot instances | Cheaper workers; keep the driver on-demand and expect occasional task retries |

#### Validate, don't guess

1. Run the job on a sample (for example one hour of data, ~4% of a day) on a small cluster.

2. Read the Spark UI: task durations, shuffle sizes, spill, GC time, skew.

3. Scale linearly to the full day and to the SLA, then add ~20–30% headroom for growth and peak days.

4. Turn on autoscaling with a sensible max so peak days don't fail and normal days don't overpay.

5. Re-check monthly — data volume grows.

#### Same volumes as a stream

Spread across 24 hours, the same data needs far less compute than a short batch window:

| Daily volume | Average rate | Peak (≈3× average) | Kafka partitions (≈10 MB/s each, with headroom) | Typical streaming cluster |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 GB | ~0.12 MB/s | ~0.4 MB/s | 3–6 | 1–2 small workers |
| 100 GB | ~1.2 MB/s | ~3.5 MB/s | 6–12 | 2 workers |
| 500 GB | ~5.8 MB/s | ~17 MB/s | 12–24 | 2–4 workers |
| 1 TB | ~11.6 MB/s | ~35 MB/s | 24–48 | 4–6 workers |
| 2 TB | ~23 MB/s | ~70 MB/s | 48–96 | 6–10 workers |

Streaming trades a big short burst for a small always-on cluster. The right choice depends on the latency the business needs, the cost of 24/7 compute, and operational effort — not just volume.

> In an interview, say the method out loud: partitions from data size → work from tasks × stages × time per task → cores from the SLA → executors of 5 cores → nodes from executors per node → memory per executor with overhead → shuffle partitions from shuffle size. Then mention skew, AQE, a sample run and autoscaling. That's what separates a real answer from a memorized number.

title: Practice project: an end-to-end mini pipeline
md:
Build this on your laptop or in Databricks Free Edition. It uses almost every concept in the handbook on data you generate yourself.

#### The scenario

An online store has **orders** (with duplicates and late updates) and **customers**. Build bronze → silver → gold tables and answer business questions.

#### Step 1: generate raw data

```python norun
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F, Window as W
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[*]").appName("practice").getOrCreate()
customers = spark.createDataFrame(
    [(1, "Asha", "Bengaluru"), (2, "Ravi", "Pune"), (3, "Meena", "Chennai"), (4, "Arjun", None)],
    "customer_id INT, name STRING, city STRING")
orders = (spark.range(1, 200_001).withColumnRenamed("id", "order_id")
  .withColumn("customer_id", (F.rand(seed=1) * 4 + 1).cast("int"))
  .withColumn("amount", F.round(F.rand(seed=2) * 5000, 2))
  .withColumn("status", F.element_at(F.array(F.lit("PLACED"), F.lit("SHIPPED"),
F.lit("DELIVERED"), F.lit("CANCELLED")),
                                     (F.rand(seed=3) * 4 + 1).cast("int")))
  .withColumn("updated_at", F.expr("timestamp('2026-01-01') + make_interval(0,0,0,0,0,0,
cast(rand(4) * 2592000 as int))")))
dupes = orders.sample(fraction=0.05, seed=5).withColumn("updated_at", F.col("updated_at") +
F.expr("INTERVAL 1 HOUR"))
raw = orders.unionByName(dupes)                       # ~5% of orders have a later second
version
raw.write.mode("overwrite").json("practice/landing/orders")
customers.write.mode("overwrite").json("practice/landing/customers")
```

#### Step 2: bronze — read raw with an explicit schema

```python norun
order_schema = "order_id LONG, customer_id INT, amount DOUBLE, status STRING, updated_at
TIMESTAMP"
bronze = (spark.read.schema(order_schema).json("practice/landing/orders")
          .withColumn("_ingest_ts", F.current_timestamp())
          .withColumn("_source_file", F.input_file_name()))
bronze.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("practice/bronze/orders")
```

#### Step 3: silver — clean, deduplicate (latest version wins), add date

```python norun
w = W.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.desc("updated_at"))
silver = (spark.read.parquet("practice/bronze/orders")
  .filter(F.col("order_id").isNotNull())
  .withColumn("amount", F.col("amount").cast("decimal(18,2)"))
  .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("rn = 1").drop("rn")
  .withColumn("order_date", F.to_date("updated_at")))
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode", "dynamic")
silver.repartition("order_date").write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("order_date").parquet("practice/silver/orders")
```

#### Step 4: gold — business tables

```python norun
cust = spark.read.schema("customer_id INT, name STRING, city
STRING").json("practice/landing/customers") \
            .fillna({"city": "UNKNOWN"})
s = spark.read.parquet("practice/silver/orders")
daily_city = (s.filter("status <> 'CANCELLED'")
  .join(F.broadcast(cust), "customer_id", "left")
  .groupBy("order_date", "city")
  .agg(F.count("*").alias("orders"), F.sum("amount").alias("revenue")))
running = daily_city.withColumn("running_revenue",
    F.sum("revenue").over(W.partitionBy("city").orderBy("order_date")
                           .rowsBetween(W.unboundedPreceding, 0)))
running.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("practice/gold/daily_city_revenue")
```

#### Step 5: check your work

```python norun
assert s.groupBy("order_id").count().filter("count > 1").count() == 0, "duplicates in silver"
print("bronze rows:", spark.read.parquet("practice/bronze/orders").count())
print("silver rows:", s.count())          # should be 200,000
spark.read.parquet("practice/gold/daily_city_revenue").orderBy("city", "order_date").show(10)
```

#### Step 6: questions to answer yourself

1. Top 3 customers by revenue in each city.

2. Month-over-month revenue growth % per city.

3. Customers with no orders in the last 7 days of the data.

4. Percentage of orders cancelled per day.

5. Open the Spark UI: how many stages did step 3 create, and why? Where are the shuffles?

6. Run `explain(mode="formatted")` on step 4. Is the customers join a broadcast join?

7. Change step 3 to use `dropDuplicates(["order_id"])` and compare totals — why can the result be wrong?

8. Rewrite steps 2–3 as a Structured Streaming job with `trigger(availableNow=True)` reading new files from the landing folder.

> Finish this project and you've used schemas, file formats, partitioned writes, deduplication with windows, broadcast joins, aggregations, running totals, data-quality checks and the Spark UI — the same toolkit as a real pipeline.

#### Configs worth knowing

| Config | Default | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` | 200 | Tasks after a shuffle |
| `spark.sql.adaptive.enabled` | true (3.2+) | AQE: coalesce, skew join, join switching |
| `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` | 10 MB | Auto broadcast limit (−1 disables) |
| `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` | 128 MB | Input partition size |
| `spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode` | static | `dynamic` to overwrite only written partitions |
| `spark.executor.memory` / `.cores` / `.memoryOverhead` | cluster- specific | Executor sizing |
| `spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled` | false (varies) | Scale executors with load |
| `spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled` | false (varies) | Faster pandas conversion |

#### Quick answers to common questions

| Question | Short answer |
|---|---|
| RDD vs DataFrame vs Dataset | RDD: objects, no schema, no optimizer; DataFrame: schema + Catalyst/Tungsten, default; Dataset: typed DataFrame, Scala/Java only |
| repartition vs coalesce | repartition = full shuffle, can increase, even sizes; coalesce = no shuffle, only decrease, can be uneven |
| cache vs persist | cache = persist(MEMORY_AND_DISK) for DataFrames; persist lets you choose the level |
| narrow vs wide | narrow: no data movement (filter, select); wide: shuffle (groupBy, join, distinct) |
| Transformation vs action | transformations are lazy and build the plan; actions (count, write, collect) run jobs |
| Job / stage / task | action → job; shuffle boundaries → stages; one task per partition per stage |
| Why is a job slow? | Compare runs in Spark UI: input growth, skew (max ≫ median task), spill, small files, too few/many partitions, Python UDFs |
| Fix skew | AQE skew join, broadcast the small side, isolate hot keys, salting |
| Fix executor OOM | More/smaller partitions, fix skew, less caching, more memoryOverhead for Python, then more memory |
| Fix driver OOM | Avoid collect/toPandas on big data, don't broadcast big tables, compact small files |
| Small files | repartition by partition column before write, coalesce, Delta OPTIMIZE / auto-compaction |
| Broadcast join limit | Default 10 MB auto; hint `broadcast()` up to what executors/driver can hold |
| dropDuplicates vs row_number | dropDuplicates keeps an arbitrary row; row_number + order lets you choose (latest) |
| union vs unionByName | union matches by position; unionByName by column name |
| Exactly-once streaming | Replayable source + checkpoint + idempotent sink (Delta / MERGE) |
| Watermark | Bound on lateness; lets Spark finalize windows and drop old state |
| Executor sizing rule | ~5 cores per executor, leave 1 core + some GB per node for OS, ~10% memoryOverhead |
| Shuffle partition sizing | ~100–200 MB per partition; let AQE coalesce |
| UDF performance | built-in functions > pandas UDF > Python UDF |

title: Remember it for life: memory hooks
md:
Facts on their own fade within days. What we remember are **stories, places, people, pictures and patterns**. This chapter turns Spark into exactly those, so a quick look brings the whole idea back.

#### Why these tricks work

| Memory principle | What it means | How this chapter uses it |
|---|---|---|
| **Stories and** **analogies** | The brain stores meaning by linking new ideas to things it already knows | Spark as a restaurant kitchen — everyone knows how a kitchen works |
| **Method of loci** **(memory palace)** | Placing ideas at locations along a familiar walk makes them easy to recall in order | A walk through the kitchen, from the entrance to the storeroom |
| **Chunking** | We hold only about 4 items at a time, so group details into small chunks | Everything grouped into threes and fours |
| **Mnemonics** | First letters or rhymes act as a hook to pull out a list | Don't Cook Everything Together, Really Careful Ingestion |
| **Vivid, emotional** **images** | Funny, strange or physical images stick better than abstract words | The lazy genius, the overloaded cook, the overflowing fridge |
| **Dual coding** | A picture plus words is remembered better than words alone | The architecture diagram plus the kitchen story |
| **Retrieval practice** | Testing yourself beats re-reading | The cover-and-recall self-test at the end |
| **Spaced repetition** | Reviewing just before you'd forget locks memory in | The 1–3–7–21 day revision plan |

#### The story: a night in the Spark Kitchen

Read this once slowly and picture each scene. Later, just walking through the kitchen in your head brings back every concept.

1. **The entrance — the order ticket.** A waiter writes down orders all evening, but the kitchen does nothing until the ticket is finally sent in. Transformations are written orders; the action is sending the ticket. (**Lazy evaluation**)

2. **The head chef's desk.** The head chef reads the whole ticket, plans the dishes and writes a step-by-step plan. The head chef is the driver; the plan is the DAG.

3. **The manager's office.** The head chef asks the restaurant manager for cooks. The manager hires them and sends them to the stations, then goes back to the office — the manager never cooks. The manager is the cluster manager; the cooks are executors.

4. **The stations.** Vegetables arrive in baskets. Each cook takes one basket at a time and works on it. Baskets are partitions; one cook on one basket is a task; several rounds of baskets are waves.

5. **Between courses — the walk.** Before the main course, every cook must carry their chopped onions to the onion station, their tomatoes to the tomato station. It's slow, noisy and everyone bumps into each other. That walk is the shuffle, and each course is a stage.

6. **The spice box.** A tiny spice box is copied and placed at every station, so no one walks to fetch spices. That's a broadcast join.

7. **The overloaded cook.** One cook got a basket ten times bigger than everyone else's. The whole kitchen waits for them. That's skew. Fix: split the big basket (salting), or let the kitchen manager rebalance it (AQE).

8. **The counter overflowing onto the floor.** When a cook's counter is full, they put food on the floor and pick it up later — it works, but slowly. That's spill to disk; too much spilling means baskets are too big.

9. **The fridge.** Dishes needed again later go in the fridge so they don't have to be cooked twice. That's cache/persist — and a full fridge with unused food just wastes space.

10. **The recipe card.** If a cook drops a dish, they don't panic — the recipe card says exactly how to remake it. That's lineage and fault tolerance.

11. **The live adjustments.** Halfway through service, the kitchen manager sees one station is idle and another is swamped, and moves work around. That's Adaptive Query Execution.

12. **The delivery counter.** Large orders go straight out of the back door to customers; only the bill comes back to the head chef. Executors write output directly to storage; only small results go to the driver.

13. **The night shift logbook.** For delivery orders arriving all night, the kitchen keeps a logbook: "last order cooked: #4,512". After a power cut, it restarts from #4,513. That's Structured Streaming with a checkpoint.

14. **The last-entry rule.** At closing, guests arriving more than 15 minutes late aren't seated, so the kitchen can finally close the evening's bill. That's a watermark.

#### One-look concept anchors

| Concept | Picture it as | One-line hook |
|---|---|---|
| Driver | Head chef with the plan | Plans and schedules, doesn't chop |
| Executor | A cook at a station | Does the real work, holds the fridge |
| Cluster manager | Restaurant manager | Hires cooks, then steps away |
| Partition | A basket of vegetables | Goldilocks size: ~128–200 MB |
| Task | One cook, one basket | One task per partition per stage |
| Stage | A course of the meal | A shuffle ends a course |
| Job | One full order ticket | One action = one job |
| Lazy evaluation | A lazy genius | Plans everything, does nothing until asked |
| Shuffle | Everyone walking ingredients across the kitchen | The most expensive thing Spark does |
| Broadcast join | A spice box at every station | Small table? Spread it |
| Sort-merge join | Both teams lining up in order to pair off | Both big? Sort and merge |
| Skew | One overloaded cook | One slow task holds up the stage |
| Salting | Splitting the giant basket into smaller ones | Spread the hot key |
| Spill | Food on the floor | Memory full → disk → slow |
| Cache | The fridge | Store only what you'll reuse |
| Lineage | The recipe card | Lost work is rebuilt, not lost |
| Catalyst | GPS planning the route | Rewrites your query before running |
| AQE | Live traffic updates | Re-plans during the run |
| Checkpoint | The night-shift logbook | Restart exactly where you stopped |
| Watermark | The last-entry time | How late is too late |
| RDD | Unlabelled sacks of ingredients | Flexible, but the chef can't plan |
| DataFrame | Labelled containers on a spreadsheet | The chef can see and optimize everything |
| Dataset | Labelled and locked containers | Typed — Scala/Java only |

#### Mnemonics cheat card

| Mnemonic | Stands for |
|---|---|
| **D·C·E·T** — Don't Cook Everything Together | **D**river, **C**luster manager, **E**xecutor, **T**ask |
| **J·S·T** — Just Split Tasks | 1 action → 1 **J**ob; 1 shuffle → new **S**tage; 1 partition → 1 **T**ask |
| Can Charlie Show The Work First? | Actions: **C**ount, **C**ollect, **S**how, **T**ake, **W**rite, **F**irst |
| Just Getting Data Organized Requires a shuffle | Wide ops: **J**oin, **G**roupBy, **D**istinct, **O**rderBy, **R**epartition |
| Narrow stays in its Lane, Wide Walks | Narrow = no data movement; wide = shuffle |
| Repartition = Reshuffle, Coalesce = Combine | repartition: full shuffle, up or down; coalesce: no shuffle, only down |
| Cache is Common, Persist lets you Pick | cache = default level; persist = choose the storage level |
| **B·A·S·H** the skew | **B**roadcast, **A**QE skew join, **S**alting, **H**andle hot keys separately |
| **R·C·I** — Really Careful Ingestion | Exactly-once = **R**eplayable source + **C**heckpoint + **I**dempotent sink |
| **5 · 1 · 10** | 5 cores per executor, leave 1 core per node, ~10% memory overhead |
| Built-in Beats Pandas Beats Python | UDF preference: built-in functions > pandas UDF > Python UDF |
| **A·O·I·E** — Always Overwrite Intentionally, Everyone | Save modes: **A**ppend, **O**verwrite, **I**gnore, **E**rror |
| Read less, Move less, Balance, No Python | The four performance rules: prune/filter, avoid shuffles, fix skew/partitions, avoid UDFs |
| To the boss vs too heavy a basket | Driver OOM = data sent **to** the driver; executor OOM = a partition too big |

#### Spark on a napkin

If you can redraw this from memory, you understand Spark:

```text
 YOUR CODE  ──►  DRIVER (head chef: plan = DAG → stages → tasks)
                    │  asks for cooks             ▲ small results only
                    ▼                             │
             CLUSTER MANAGER (hires, then leaves) │
                    │ launches                    │
      ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐               │
   EXECUTOR      EXECUTOR      EXECUTOR  ──────────┘  (tasks talk to the driver)
   baskets       baskets       baskets
      └──── shuffle (walk between stations) ────┘
                    │
      STORAGE (read input, write output directly)
```

#### Self-test: cover the right column

Cover the answers, say each one out loud, then check. Saying it beats reading it.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What happens when you call `filter()`? | Nothing runs — it's added to the plan (lazy) |
| What starts a job? | An action (count, collect, show, take, write) |
| What splits a job into stages? | A shuffle |
| How many tasks in a stage? | One per partition |
| Who processes the data — driver or executors? | Executors |
| Does the cluster manager move your data? | No — it only allocates resources |
| Cheapest way to join a 50 MB table to a 2 TB table? | Broadcast the 50 MB table |
| One task runs 20× longer than the rest — why? | Skew |
| Four ways to fix skew? | Broadcast, AQE, salting, handle hot keys separately |
| repartition vs coalesce? | Reshuffle (up/down, full shuffle) vs combine (down only, no shuffle) |
| When should you cache? | When a DataFrame is reused by several actions and expensive to recompute |
| Three parts of exactly-once streaming? | Replayable source, checkpoint, idempotent sink |
| What does a watermark do? | Limits lateness so windows can close and old state is dropped |
| Typical executor size? | ~5 cores, leave 1 core per node for the OS, ~10% memory overhead |
| Driver OOM — most common cause? | collect/toPandas or broadcasting a big table |

#### Revision plan (spaced repetition)

| When | What to do | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Day 1 | Read the kitchen story; redraw "Spark on a napkin" from memory | 20 min |
| Day 3 | Self-test table; re-read only the questions you missed | 10 min |
| Day 7 | Explain Spark architecture and a shuffle out loud to a friend (or record yourself) | 10 min |
| Day 21 | Mnemonics card + self-test; solve two PySpark problems from memory | 20 min |
| Before an interview | Kitchen story + napkin drawing + cheat sheet | 15 min |

> The fastest way to own a concept is to teach it. If you can explain Spark using the kitchen story to someone who has never coded, you will never forget it — and you'll explain it clearly in any interview.

title: Glossary
md:
Plain-language definitions of the terms used in this handbook.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Action** | An operation that returns a result or writes data (`count`, `show`, `collect`, `write`) and makes Spark actually run |
| **AQE (Adaptive Query** **Execution)** | Spark re-optimizing a query while it runs, using real data sizes (merging small partitions, fixing skew, switching to broadcast joins) |
| **Broadcast join** | Copying a small table to every executor so the big table doesn't need to be shuffled |
| **Bucketing** | Pre-splitting a table into a fixed number of files by hashing a column, to speed up joins on that column |
| **Cache / persist** | Keeping a computed DataFrame in memory (and/or disk) so later actions reuse it |
| **Catalyst** | Spark's query optimizer that rewrites your plan into a faster one |
| **Checkpoint** **(streaming)** | Folder where a streaming query stores its progress (offsets, state) so it can restart where it stopped |
| **Cluster manager** | System that gives Spark machines/containers: YARN, Kubernetes, Standalone, Databricks |
| **Coalesce** | Reducing the number of partitions without a full shuffle |
| **Column pruning** | Reading only the columns a query needs from columnar files |
| **DAG** | Directed Acyclic Graph — the plan of stages and their dependencies |
| **DataFrame** | A distributed table with named, typed columns — the main PySpark API |
| **Delta Lake** | Table format that adds ACID transactions, MERGE, time travel and schema enforcement to Parquet files |
| **Driver** | The process running your program; plans the work and schedules tasks |
| **Dynamic partition** **overwrite** | Overwriting only the partitions present in the output, not the whole table |
| **Executor** | A worker process on a cluster node that runs tasks and stores cached data |
| **Explain plan** | Text showing how Spark will execute a query (`df.explain()`) |
| **Idempotent** | Running the same job twice gives the same result as running it once — safe reruns |
| **Lazy evaluation** | Transformations only build a plan; work happens at an action |
| **Lineage** | The recorded chain of transformations; used to recompute lost partitions |
| **memoryOverhead** | Extra memory outside the JVM heap for Python workers, buffers and JVM overhead |
| **Narrow transformation** | Each output partition needs only one input partition (filter, select) — no shuffle |
| **Partition** | A chunk of data processed by one task |
| **Term** | **Meaning** |
| **Partition pruning** | Skipping folders/partitions that a filter rules out |
| **Predicate pushdown** | Sending filters down to the file reader so it can skip data using file statistics |
| **Repartition** | Changing the number of partitions (or partitioning by a column) with a full shuffle |
| **RDD** | Resilient Distributed Dataset — Spark's original low-level API of distributed objects |
| **Salting** | Adding a random number to a skewed key to spread its rows over several partitions |
| **Schema** | Column names and data types of a DataFrame |
| **Shuffle** | Redistributing data across executors by key; needed for joins, groupBy, distinct, orderBy |
| **Skew** | Uneven data distribution — a few keys or partitions much larger than the rest, so a few tasks run far longer |
| **Spill** | Writing data from memory to disk because a task ran out of execution memory |
| **Stage** | A group of tasks that run without a shuffle; shuffles split jobs into stages |
| **Structured Streaming** | Spark's streaming engine that runs DataFrame queries incrementally on new data |
| **Task** | The smallest unit of work: one partition processed by one core in one stage |
| **Transformation** | An operation that defines a new DataFrame (select, filter, join) without running anything yet |
| **Trigger** | When a streaming query processes the next batch (every N minutes, once, availableNow) |
| **Tungsten** | Spark's execution engine improvements: compact binary memory format, code generation |
| **UDF** | User-Defined Function written in Python/Scala; slower than built-in functions |
| **Watermark** | A limit on how late events can arrive in a stream, so Spark can finalize windows and drop old state |
| **Wave** | One round of tasks when there are more partitions than cores (1,000 tasks on 100 cores = 10 waves) |
| **Wide transformation** | Output partitions need data from many input partitions — causes a shuffle |
| **Window function** | Computes a value for each row from related rows (rank, lag, running total) without collapsing rows |

> Learn these words well: in interviews and design discussions, explaining a problem with the right term — "the join stage is skewed and spilling" — immediately shows you understand Spark.

**— Sagar**
